issues.description: Command names use inconsistent plural/singular convention versus existing commands
issues.detail: Existing commands are `quickmark_save`, `quickmark_load`, `bookmark_add`, `bookmark_load` — singular noun. The new commands are `quickmarks_reload` / `bookmarks_reload` — plural. The data hasn't changed shape, so the naming shouldn't either. Pick `quickmark_reload` / `bookmark_reload` to match. Command names are a public data structure too.

issues.description: Two near-identical command methods where one parameterized helper would do
issues.detail: `quickmarks_reload` and `bookmarks_reload` differ only in the objreg key and the message string. A single small helper, or registering both against a shared implementation that takes the manager name, would remove the copy. Not load-bearing — two six-line methods is fine — but it's the kind of duplication that grows if a third mark type ever appears.

issues.description: reload() is not atomic: clears marks before reading, leaving empty state on parse failure
issues.detail: `reload()` does `self.marks.clear()` and then re-reads from disk. If `_init_lineparser` or parsing raises, the in-memory marks are gone and the user is left with nothing until restart. The right data shape is: build a new OrderedDict from disk, then swap it in on success. That makes the algorithm obvious (parse → assign) and makes failure non-destructive.

issues.description: _init_lineparser name implies one-shot init but is now re-run on reload
issues.detail: `_init_lineparser` reads like construction-time setup (the underscore-prefix and `_init_` name both signal it). Calling it from `reload()` works because the subclasses happen to be idempotent, but the contract isn't stated. Either rename to `_open_lineparser` / `_load_lineparser`, or split construction from reading. Names are part of the data structure; making them honest costs nothing.

issues.description: Test doesn't exercise save-manager interaction after reload
issues.detail: `test_reload` verifies marks are replaced and `changed` is emitted, which is the core. It doesn't check that a subsequent modification still saves correctly — i.e. that reloading didn't break the save-manager wiring. A one-line follow-up (mutate and assert the save path) would make the test cover the whole filter: read → mutate → write.

Both new `.feature` scenarios are written as `Scenario:` with no title. Other scenarios in the file are named ("Saving a quickmark", etc.). The scenario name is the documentation; leaving it blank makes failures less legible. "Reloading bookmarks" / "Reloading quickmarks" would do.

review.summary: SMALL-AND-COMPOSABLE overall — the refactor extracts the disk-read into a `reload()` method on `UrlMarkManager` and reuses it from `__init__`, which is the right shape: one data structure (the on-disk file), one transform (parse), one mutation (`self.marks`). Two real concerns: `reload()` is not atomic (clear-then-read leaves marks empty on parse failure — build new dict and swap), and the two new command methods are near-duplicates that could share an implementation. Naming nits: the new commands break the existing singular convention (`quickmark_save`/`bookmark_add`), and `_init_lineparser` reads like one-shot init but is now called repeatedly. Nothing here is TOO-CLEVER or TOO-MUCH-FRAMEWORK — it's a clean, small change. Fix the atomicity issue; the rest are P2 polish.
